common_name: Ivory Silhouette Chinese Fringetree (Narrow Columnar Form)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; this narrow, upright selection fits tight side-yards and street-tree strips where the broad-spreading straight species would be too wide.

directions: Give Ivory Silhouette moist, well-drained soil and a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade for the cleanest foliage and heaviest bloom. Selected for its distinctly narrow, upright, almost columnar silhouette, this cultivar carries the same frothy, fragrant clusters of thread-like white flowers as the species each late spring, but on a much tighter frame that works where space is limited. Its glossy, leathery leaves hold their color through summer heat without scorching, and the tidy habit means little pruning is needed beyond removing the occasional wayward shoot that breaks the columnar line. Because it is more heat-tolerant and adaptable to a wider soil pH range than native white fringetree, it is a dependable choice for compact urban and suburban plantings across the warmer half of its range.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Marley's Pink Parasol Japanese Snowbell (Deep Rose-Pink Weeping Snowbell)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this patented weeping selection is grown as much for its cascading form as for its unusually saturated pink flower color.

directions: Site Marley's Pink Parasol in moist, acidic, well-drained soil with afternoon shade, since Japanese snowbell foliage stresses quickly in dry heat or alkaline ground. This selection stands apart from other weeping snowbell cultivars by its markedly deeper rose-pink flower color, a shade or two more saturated than the pale blush of older pink-flowered forms, and the pendulous branches display the dangling, bell-shaped blooms to striking effect in late spring. The gracefully cascading habit stays smaller and more shrub-like than an upright snowbell tree, making it well suited to a specimen spot near a patio, along a shaded path, or underplanted with spring bulbs and ferns that enjoy the same dappled light. Mulch generously to keep roots cool and moist, and prune only lightly, right after flowering, to preserve the natural weeping silhouette.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Evening Light Japanese Snowbell (Dark Purple-Leaved Snowbell)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; foliage color develops best with some direct morning sun rather than deep, constant shade.

directions: Give Evening Light moist, acidic, well-drained soil in a spot with a few hours of morning sun and shelter from harsh afternoon heat; strong dappled light brings out the darkest leaf color without scorching. Its emerging foliage unfurls in deep purple-black tones that hold through the growing season, throwing the small pink-blushed, bell-shaped white flowers of late spring into sharp, striking contrast against the near-black leaves. As a specimen it reads almost like a small ornamental plum from a distance, then rewards a closer look with the same fragrant, dangling snowbell flowers typical of the species. Water regularly during establishment and dry spells, since Japanese snowbell has shallow roots that suffer in prolonged drought, and mulch to conserve moisture and keep the root zone cool.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this Gulf Coast Florida panhandle variant is even more shade-tolerant than typical Halesia diptera and thrives as a true understory tree.

directions: Plant this variety in humus-rich, consistently moist, acidic soil in partial to fairly deep shade, mimicking the shaded ravine slopes and bluff woodlands of the Florida panhandle and adjacent Gulf Coast where it grows wild beneath a closed canopy. Compared with typical two-wing silverbell, the giant-flowered variety produces notably larger, showier bell-shaped white flowers, some nearly twice the length of the species, borne in dangling clusters along bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge. Its two-winged fruits and multi-stemmed, small-tree habit otherwise match the species, and it shares the same intolerance of drought, compacted soil, and root disturbance during transplanting. Because it naturally tolerates deeper shade than either H. carolina or typical H. diptera, it is one of the better native flowering trees for the darker corners of a woodland garden, and it pairs well with other shade-loving natives such as oakleaf hydrangea and native azaleas.
sources: Dirr, M.A. Manual of Woody Landscape Plants
Atlas of Florida Plants / Florida Native Plant Society
